title: Propagate plants in a variety of situations

lessons.title: Propagation facilities and planning
lessons.html:
Propagation in different situations

Plants are propagated in many settings: commercial vegetable seedling nurseries, fruit tree nurseries, ornamental nurseries, forestry nurseries, on-farm propagation for orchards and vineyards, community food gardens and indigenous plant rehabilitation projects. At NQF level 4 you must choose and manage methods suited to the crop, purpose, scale and facilities.

Matching method to situation

SituationTypical methods
Vegetable seedling nurserySeed sown in plug trays in a tunnel, transplanted at the correct stage
Citrus or avocado nurserySeedling or clonal rootstocks, budded or grafted with certified scion material
Vineyard establishmentGrafted vines from certified nurseries; hardwood cuttings for rootstocks
Sweet potato or cassava productionVine or stem cuttings from clean mother plants
PotatoesCertified seed potatoes (tubers)
Ornamentals and herbsSoftwood and semi-hardwood cuttings, division, layering
Bananas, some berriesTissue-cultured plantlets, hardened off in the nursery
Indigenous rehabilitationLocally collected seed (with permits where needed), cuttings, division

Facilities and environment

  • Propagation structures: tunnels or greenhouses with shade cloth, mist or fog systems for cuttings, heated benches for bottom heat where required.
  • Hardening-off areas: gradually expose young plants to outdoor conditions before planting out.
  • Media: clean, well-drained mixes such as composted bark, coir, peat alternatives, perlite or vermiculite; sterilised or new to avoid damping-off fungi.
  • Water: clean, tested water; poor water can spread disease or cause salt damage.

Planning

Work backwards from the planting-out date: number of plants needed, plus a margin for losses; time needed for each stage; space, media, trays and labour. Order certified seed, rootstocks or budwood in good time, since certified material is often booked well in advance.

Plant health certification

For many crops, such as citrus, deciduous fruit, grapevines and potatoes, industry certification schemes supply disease-tested material. Using certified material protects the farm from viruses and other diseases that cannot be cured once planted.

lessons.title: Carrying out and managing propagation
lessons.html:
Seed propagation in trays

  1. Fill trays evenly with moist medium; do not compact.
  2. Sow at the depth and number per cell recommended for the crop.
  3. Label trays: crop, cultivar, date and batch.
  4. Germinate at the right temperature; some nurseries use germination rooms.
  5. Move to light as soon as seedlings emerge to prevent stretching.
  6. Water carefully and feed lightly as seedlings develop.
  7. Harden off before dispatch or transplanting.

Cuttings

  • Take cuttings from healthy, true-to-type, well-watered mother plants, early in the day.
  • Use sharp, disinfected tools; cut below a node.
  • Remove lower leaves; reduce large leaves to limit water loss.
  • Dip in rooting hormone where appropriate, following the product label.
  • Insert in medium under mist or high humidity; provide bottom heat if required.
  • Check for rooting, then pot on and harden off.

Budding and grafting

  • Use certified budwood and vigorous rootstocks of the right size.
  • Match cambium layers precisely and wrap firmly with budding tape.
  • Work in shade and quickly to prevent drying.
  • Unwrap or force buds at the correct time; remove rootstock shoots (suckers).

Tissue-cultured plantlets

Acclimatise gradually from high humidity to normal nursery conditions; they are very sensitive to drying and disease at this stage.

Nursery hygiene and pest control

  • Clean benches, trays and tools between batches.
  • Footbaths at entrances; restrict visitors.
  • Scout for damping-off, aphids, whitefly, thrips and fungus gnats.
  • Use IPM and only registered products per label.

Quality control and records

Record batch numbers, sowing or grafting dates, germination or take percentage, losses and dispatch dates. Inspect plants before dispatch for root development, vigour, true-to-type appearance and pest freedom.

Safety

Grafting knives demand careful technique. Wear gloves and masks for media dust, hormones and disinfectants as directed by labels. Keep electrical heating and misting equipment safe around water.

Key points

  • Choose propagation methods to suit crop, purpose, scale and facilities.
  • Plan backwards from planting-out date and order certified material early.
  • Use clean media, water and tools to prevent disease.
  • Follow correct technique for seed, cuttings, grafting and tissue culture plantlets.
  • Harden off plants and keep batch records for quality control.

quiz.question: Why should certified propagation material be used for crops like citrus and grapevines?

options.text: It protects against viruses and diseases that cannot be cured after planting
It does not need hardening off

quiz.question: What is the purpose of hardening off?

options.text: To gradually expose young plants to outdoor conditions

quiz.question: How should a nursery plan propagation timing?

options.text: Work backwards from the planting-out date
Sow all crops on the same day

quiz.question: Where should cuttings be made on the stem?
What causes seedlings to stretch after emergence?

options.text: Not moving them to light soon enough
